name: Marco Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Marco, 43, and a junior electrician after moving out of catering stores. I've a vocational certificate, still struggle to work out which test to ask for on an unfamiliar fault, and a senior checks and signs off installations. My employer pays above the usual rate; my partner Eva maintains park gardens, we've children aged nine and twelve, a mortgage, and ten months of expenses saved. Plenty of electrical firms work nearby, and I sometimes use AI to explain a diagram after a colleague has shown me how to check it; I like finishing something real, but dislike pretending I've understood an instruction when I need it repeated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a little help with paperwork sounds useful without changing the whole reason I'm here. I want to become better at the electrical work, not better at describing myself as ready for the future. A normal paid week would suit me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our regular wages cover the mortgage and bills, and ten months of savings makes a quiet spell manageable. I know I'm still learning, but I don't feel one confused morning would put the house at risk. There are other firms nearby to approach if I ever needed to look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my supervised electrical shifts now and through the next year. This month I'd ask my senior to watch me explain one familiar circuit each week during normal paid work, so I could find the gaps before the next job. I'd keep using an occasional checked AI explanation, without buying a subscription or changing our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and glad I can focus on getting the next task right. The savings don't make me skilled. They make it easier to admit I'm not there yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do when an instruction still makes no sense?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop and ask the senior to explain it another way, then repeat it back. I wouldn't treat my age as a reason I ought to know without asking. The senior still needs to check the installation, whatever I've said about understanding it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner about an ordinary day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Eva about a small thing I'd finally understood, then get on with the children's homework and dinner. My partner has practical puzzles at work too. It's nice when the day's story isn't only a list of things we should be worried about.

say: I'd welcome **modest paperwork help** while concentrating on learning electrical work.
I'd prefer a **normal paid week** to claims that I have mastered the whole future.
think: Regular wages and **ten months saved** make the mortgage and an ordinary quiet spell manageable.
Nearby employers give options, while financial room lets me admit **learning gaps** without immediate fear for the house.
do: Keep **supervised electrical shifts** through the next year.
Request a **weekly circuit explanation** inside normal paid work, retaining checked occasional AI study.
feel: **Calm** with room to learn, able to admit uncertainty without confusing savings with electrical competence.
S0.quote: The savings don't make me skilled.
fieldNote: He separates **financial strength** from junior electrical ability, preserving certificate-level education and senior sign-off.
His occasional **AI explanations** remain checked and limited to learning rather than replacing supervision or installation tests.

steps.text: Keep supervised electrical shifts and checked occasional study within paid work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see the new parts list work on real jobs before depending on it. I'd use a demonstrated tool, but I wouldn't call my senior unnecessary because the screen writes a tidy explanation. Someone still needs to check what I've actually understood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own hours could shrink if the firm keeps fewer juniors when ordering and planning get quicker. Most of my work is physical, but the firm's choice about a helper isn't divided neatly into thinking minutes and hand minutes. Ten months saved gives us control if that happens, not a reason to call it harmless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask my senior to demonstrate the approved AI parts-list tool during two normal paid shifts. Over the first year I'd check it against twelve jobs with the senior approving every order, and record errors before asking to use it more often. I'd also redirect the 60 monthly upgrade fund for my bicycle into emergency savings while our wages covered the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the hours, and willing to test a useful change. I don't need the tool to fail to prove I have a place. I'd like the firm to say what happens to the people when a task gets quicker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask about your hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether basic shifts would stay whole, and when we'd hear if that changed. I wouldn't ask for a promise nobody could keep. A clear answer about the next rota would be more useful than praise for adapting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the trial produced confident but wrong lists?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the error in the record and ask why the list missed the actual job requirement. If the checking took longer than the old method, I'd say so. I can be open to the tool and still conclude that this use hasn't proved itself.

say: I'd judge **real job results** before depending on a neat parts list.
I'd keep **senior checking** essential, even when a screen explains the work clearly.
think: My **junior hours** could shrink if faster ordering leads the firm to retain fewer helpers.
Our **ten-month reserve** gives control over a shock without making reduced wages harmless.
do: Learn the **approved AI parts tool** during two normal paid shifts after demonstration.
Check **twelve job lists** with every order approved by the senior.
Redirect the bicycle **60 monthly** upgrade fund into emergency savings while bills remain covered.
feel: **Anxious and open**, willing to test improvements while asking how the firm will treat affected workers.
S1.quote: I don't need the tool to fail to prove I have a place.
fieldNote: He identifies **employment decisions** about junior places rather than claiming most of the electrician's physical work is already automated.
The **demonstrated trial** keeps both paid shifts and senior approval, consistent with steady rather than impulsive adoption.

steps.text: Learn approved AI parts tool in two paid shifts, with senior demonstration and order checks
Redirect the bicycle upgrade 60 monthly into emergency savings while bills stay covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the thinking side changes in 2028, and capable robots reach physical work around 2031. I wouldn't tell the family that getting into a hands-on trade settled everything. I'd ask the firm which paid junior duties it expected to keep and what notice we'd get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could shrink well before the later robots if the firm stops keeping so many learners, and fitting work could face more pressure around 2031. Eva's garden work isn't guaranteed safe from capable physical machines either. We've a good reserve and local employers to approach, but I would need to check actual paid work rather than count employers as vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd pay for a weekend fault-testing workshop from our separate study budget, keeping all basic shifts and emergency savings intact. In 2029 I'd apply for actual paid supervised repair vacancies only with written pay and hours covering the mortgage and essentials. We'd keep moving the bicycle fund's 60 monthly into emergency savings only while ordinary bills stayed covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can see experiments small enough to afford. I don't expect the workshop to make me an expert or the local job list to stay full forever. I want to use the reserve to keep choices open, not to avoid looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check about the weekend workshop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the tutor what I still needed supervision for and whether the workshop matched the actual advertised duties. I'd keep the practice separate from any authority to sign off installations. A weekend is enough to learn something, not enough to become a different grade of electrician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a new job offer have to contain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the basic pay and hours in writing, along with real supervision. I wouldn't leave my present wage for a higher rate attached to uncertain hours. The move needs to cover our mortgage and essentials, not just sound more advanced.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking work** from capable robots reaching physical tasks around 2031.
I'd ask about **paid junior duties** and notice rather than call a hands-on trade permanent protection.
think: My **junior hours** could shrink before robots add later pressure to physical fitting work.
A strong reserve and nearby employers give options, but **actual vacancies** and both household wages still need checking.
do: Fund a **weekend workshop** from the separate study budget, retaining basic shifts and emergency savings.
Seek **2029 supervised vacancies** only on written pay and hours covering mortgage and essentials.
Save the bicycle **60 monthly** only while ordinary bills remain covered.
feel: **Anxious with affordable experiments**, refusing to treat a short workshop or local employers as guaranteed replacement income.
S2.quote: A weekend is enough to learn something, not enough to become a different grade of electrician.
fieldNote: His **course conditions** preserve a separate study budget, all basic paid shifts and the emergency reserve.
The **job search** requires actual paid supervision and essential-covering written terms; the workshop never changes his present sign-off limits.

steps.text: Fund weekend electrical fault-testing study separately, retaining basic shifts and emergency savings
Accept 2029 supervised electrical work only with written pay and hours covering mortgage and essentials
Save the bicycle fund’s 60 monthly only while ordinary bills stay covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to check a course against real paid work instead of calling enrolment the answer. Thinking AGI arrives in 2031 and capable robots around 2034. I'd still ask about junior hours now, because a company can change its staffing plans before a machine arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could shrink during that preparation, though I've time and money to test another route before the physical machines spread. I wouldn't assume a short workshop made me more employable until an employer offered actual paid supervision. The mortgage needs wages through the preparation years as well as afterwards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the weekend workshop now from the separate study budget, keeping every basic shift and emergency savings intact. We'd save the bicycle 60 monthly while bills stayed covered and review actual costs after a year. During 2032 I'd apply for paid supervised vacancies only with written pay and hours covering the mortgage and essentials, retaining the present job until an acceptable offer existed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the choices, but not hurried into buying the biggest course. I can try one small thing while the wage keeps coming. If it doesn't help, I'd rather learn that cheaply than keep paying to defend the first decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the workshop did not improve your options?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether I could do the actual tasks better under supervision and whether vacancies asked for those skills. If the answer was no, I'd keep the experience but stop buying further courses in that line. Being open to change doesn't mean agreeing every proposed change is worthwhile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you review after the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eva and I would check actual paid hours and essentials, then decide whether the bicycle contribution still belonged in the emergency account. If necessary costs had risen, we'd reduce the transfer rather than borrow to keep it going. The household budget matters more than my promise to a savings target.

say: I'd compare **course skills** with real work rather than treat enrolment itself as the solution.
I'd ask about **junior staffing now**, since employers can prepare before capable machines arrive.
think: My **hours could shrink** during preparation, although money and time allow a limited test of alternatives.
A workshop isn't replacement income until an employer offers **actual paid work** with appropriate supervision.
do: Take **weekend study** from separate funds, keeping every basic shift and emergency savings intact.
Save the bicycle **60 monthly** while bills stay covered, reviewing costs after one year.
Seek **2032 supervised vacancies** only on written pay and hours covering mortgage and essentials.
feel: **Anxious without haste**, able to test one small change and stop paying if the evidence doesn't support more.
S3.quote: The mortgage needs wages through the preparation years as well as afterwards.
fieldNote: He sees **preparatory staffing risk** as a possible personal income change even before physical robots arrive.
Study retains **separate funds and shifts**, and the saving transfer remains affordable rather than being financed by hidden borrowing.

steps.text: Fund weekend electrical fault-testing study separately, retaining basic shifts and emergency savings
Save the bicycle fund’s 60 monthly only while ordinary bills stay covered
Accept 2032 supervised electrical work only with written pay and hours covering mortgage and essentials

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends ten years is enough to try a small change without making the whole household live inside a forecast. I'd keep an annual work and budget check. I don't want to confuse a busy course calendar with having a workable life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our wages and mortgage feel secure over the next few years in this picture, and there's time to find out what actually helps me improve. I'll be 53 when thinking AGI arrives in 2036, still needing work when robots follow around 2039. I'd keep the later question open without assuming today's junior job lasts unchanged forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the weekend workshop now from the separate study budget, retaining every basic shift and the emergency reserve. We'd redirect the bicycle 60 for a year only while bills were covered, then review actual hours, costs and vacancies annually. In 2037 I'd apply for actual paid supervised work only with written pay and hours covering mortgage and essentials, keeping the current job unless a suitable offer existed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later work, but secure enough now to enjoy learning in pieces. I can still help the children build something at the weekend without turning the afternoon into a lesson about being employable. I'd like preparation to leave some ordinary life intact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you act sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring forward the advice or vacancy checks if either wage fell or real equipment orders changed staffing. A yearly reminder isn't a reason to ignore a change in March. I'd prefer to act on our actual hours than on another dramatic video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide whether further study was affordable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd agree any extra study spending with Eva before paying, including what hours it used. If it cost basic wages or emergency savings, we'd stop and review instead of calling it automatically worthwhile. I want a proven next step, not a permanent subscription to being prepared.

say: I'd use **ten years** for limited experiments without making the household live inside a forecast.
I'd keep a **yearly work check** rather than measure preparation by a crowded course calendar.
think: Our **near-term wages** and mortgage feel secure, with time to judge what actually improves my work.
At **53 in 2036**, I'll still need future earnings, without assuming the present job lasts unchanged.
do: Fund the **weekend workshop** separately while retaining every basic shift and emergency savings.
Save the bicycle **60 monthly** for one year only while bills stay covered, then review annually.
Seek **2037 supervised work** only on written pay and hours covering mortgage and essentials, retaining current work without an acceptable offer.
feel: **Uneasy about later work**, while secure enough now for gradual learning and ordinary family weekends.
S4.quote: I want a proven next step, not a permanent subscription to being prepared.
fieldNote: His milder mood reflects **stated near-term security**, while age and mortgage obligations keep future earnings relevant.
All study preserves **basic shifts and reserves**; any further spending needs household agreement rather than becoming an automatic new commitment.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because junior hours could shrink before the later machines reach the physical work, leaving less time to check another route. Clear notice, supervised vacancies with real written hours and small courses that don't cost basic wages would help. I'd rather keep the mortgage paid during a modest experiment than gamble the reserve on a better job title.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether having savings makes it embarrassing to admit I still need help. Sometimes it does, as if financial room ought to have bought confidence too. I can afford a mistake in a course choice more easily than a mistake in someone's wiring, so the checking still matters.

headlineQuote: I'd rather keep the mortgage paid during a modest experiment than gamble the reserve on a better job title.
portrait: At **43**, Marco is a junior electrician with a vocational certificate, higher pay, and ten months of household expenses saved.
He and **Eva**, his gardening partner, have two school-age children and a mortgage, with plentiful nearby electrical employers.
He uses **AI occasionally** after demonstrations and checks new methods against real tasks, retaining senior supervision and senior installation sign-off.
Strong savings permit **small experiments**, while possible junior-hours cuts remain personal risks and later job offers must cover household essentials.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves less time to check another paid route if junior hours shrink before later physical robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear notice**, real supervised vacancies with written hours, and affordable small courses preserving basic wages would help.
